messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

I would like to ask a question about adjustment of error terms in nested designs.

I have two fixed variables (x1 and x2), both of them nested within populations (random effect).

I fitted the model as follows:

fit <- lm.rrpp (Y ~ pop/(x1 + x2), SS.type = "III",  data = mydata.df, print.progress = FALSE, iter = 999)

How should I calculate the F-value for “pop” when adjusting anova error terms, using “MS pop:x1” or “MS pop:x2”?

Actually, I’m not interested in differences among populations but among the fixed factors within each of them (without interaction), but I did not find any example similar to this situation and I’m afraid I’m missing something.

Thank you in advance,

Best,

Lucía

messages.body_plain:
Lucia,

Mathematically, one cannot have 2 ‘error’ terms in a linear model or anova. One has multiple factors and then a single error term (residual error typically). In certain situations we call other factors the ‘error’, such as in a nested model (yes I am aware that another morphometrics package has pull-down options for 2 ‘error’ terms in a linear model; which is very unfortunate and confusing wording).

About the closest one can come to incorporating 2 variables as the error is to generate a new factor from X1 and X2 like:

‘interaction(x1,x2)’

Dean

The example Dean suggested warrants a worked example, I believe, as it might help to show some interesting patterns.  The “Pupfish” data in RRPP offer a good example, as they also have a population factor, plus one other factor (sex).  We can just make up an additional factor for the purpose of illustration.  Here is the first part of the example, showing how the interaction function can be used to combine factors:

> library(RRPP)
> data("Pupfish")
> x1 <- pupfish$Sex
> set.seed(1979)
> x2 <- factor(sample(c(0, 1), length(x1), replace = TRUE))
> x1x2 <- interaction(x1, x2)
>
> Pupfish$x1 <- x1
> Pupfish$x2 <- x2
> Pupfish$x1x2 <- x1x2
>
> fit1 <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ Pop / (x1 + x2),
+                 data = Pupfish)
> anova(fit1)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq       F       Z Pr(>F)
Pop        1 0.008993 0.0089927 0.15964 15.8980  3.9590  0.001 **
Pop:x1     2 0.019370 0.0096850 0.34385 17.1220  4.5360  0.001 **
Pop:x2     2 0.000819 0.0004094 0.01454  0.7238 -0.6528  0.742
Residuals 48 0.027151 0.0005657 0.48198
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = coords ~ Pop/(x1 + x2), data = Pupfish)
>
> fit2 <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ Pop / (x1x2),
+                 data = Pupfish)
> anova(fit2)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
Pop        1 0.008993 0.0089927 0.15964 15.602 3.9328  0.001 **
Pop:x1x2   6 0.020826 0.0034710 0.36970  6.022 5.0434  0.001 **
Residuals 46 0.026514 0.0005764 0.47067
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = coords ~ Pop/(x1x2), data = Pupfish)
>

So there are two things to notice here (using type I SS):

1. The residual SS is the same whether using x1 + x2 or the combined factor, x1x2.
2. The SS for population is the same
3. The SS for Pop:x1x2 is not the sum of the SS for Pop:x1 and SS for Pop:x2.  (If instead of using Pop / (x1 + x2), Pop / (x1 * x2) was used, so the variables could fully interact, then the SS for Pop:x1x2 would be the sum of SS for Pop:x1 + Pop:x2 + Pop:x1:x2.)

So, if in the second analysis, F was recalculated, thusly:

> anova(fit2, error = c("Pop:x1x2", "Residuals"))

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)
Pop        1 0.008993 0.0089927 0.15964 2.2882 1.1764  0.134
Pop:x1x2   6 0.023580 0.0039300 0.41858 7.6084 5.8230  0.001 **
Residuals 46 0.023760 0.0005165 0.42178
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = coords ~ Pop/(x1x2), data = Pupfish)

one could create an ANOVA table for publication that has the first row of this table and the last three rows of the first ANOVA table for Pop:x1, Pop:x2, and Residuals, and it would be okay.  The SS would add up the same.

But what if one also wanted x1 and x2 to be factors in the model.  We can do that too:

> fit3 <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ x1 + x2 + Pop / (x1 + x2),
+                 data = Pupfish)
> anova(fit3)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)
x1         1 0.015780 0.0157802 0.28012 28.9808 4.8093  0.001 **
x2         1 0.000719 0.0007195 0.01277  1.3213 0.7530  0.220
Pop        1 0.008902 0.0089015 0.15802 16.3479 4.6337  0.001 **
x1:Pop     1 0.003445 0.0034447 0.06115  6.3264 3.6248  0.001 **
x2:Pop     1 0.001351 0.0013507 0.02398  2.4806 1.8250  0.033 *
Residuals 48 0.026136 0.0005445 0.46396
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = coords ~ x1 + x2 + Pop/(x1 + x2), data = Pupfish)
>
> fit4 <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ x1 + x2 + Pop +Pop:x1x2,
+                 data = Pupfish)
Warning:
This is not an error!  It is a friendly warning.

Because variables in the linear model are redundant,
the linear model design has been truncated (via QR decomposition).

Final X columns (rank): 8

Use options(warn = -1) to turn off these warnings.

> anova(fit4)

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)
x1         1 0.015780 0.0157802 0.28012 30.5505 4.9074  0.001 **
x2         1 0.000719 0.0007195 0.01277  1.3929 0.8448  0.193
Pop        1 0.008902 0.0089015 0.15802 17.2334 4.7028  0.001 **
Pop:x1x2   4 0.007171 0.0017928 0.12730  3.4709 4.4570  0.001 **
Residuals 46 0.023760 0.0005165 0.42178
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = coords ~ x1 + x2 + Pop + Pop:x1x2, data = Pupfish)
>

Notice that:
1. The SS for Pop remained constant
2. The residual SS for fit4 remained constant with fit2 because the residual degrees of freedom in fit4 matched fit2.  (Not the case for fit3, but could have been if we included x1:x2:Pop in the model, by changing Pop / (x1 + x2) to Pop / (x1 * x2).)

So, with fit4 we could update the ANOVA as,

> anova(fit4, error = c("Residuals",
+                       "Residuals",
+                       "Pop:x1x2",
+                       "Residuals"))

Analysis of Variance, using Residual Randomization
Permutation procedure: Randomization of null model residuals
Number of permutations: 1000
Estimation method: Ordinary Least Squares
Sums of Squares and Cross-products: Type I
Effect sizes (Z) based on F distributions

          Df       SS        MS     Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)
x1         1 0.015780 0.0157802 0.28012 30.5505 4.9074  0.001 **
x2         1 0.000719 0.0007195 0.01277  1.3929 0.8448  0.193
Pop        1 0.008902 0.0089015 0.15802  4.9650 2.4032  0.005 **
Pop:x1x2   4 0.007171 0.0017928 0.12730  3.4709 4.4570  0.001 **
Residuals 46 0.023760 0.0005165 0.42178
Total     53 0.056333
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Call: lm.rrpp(f1 = coords ~ x1 + x2 + Pop + Pop:x1x2, data = Pupfish)
>

This effectively allows one to combine factors in error terms.  It would be nice to be able to write something like,

error = c(“x1 + x2”,…)

but pulling this off would be a programming nightmare, which even if it worked in some cases would not be foolproof in others.  Rather, having a direct match between terms that appear in the ANOVA table functions well, even if it means tricking R to do the same thing with variables that are combinations of others.

My only additional suggestion, following on Dean’s, is to recognize that interaction(x1, x2) means x1 + x2 + x1:x2, not just x1 + x2.  If you want the math to work out the best, use Pop / (x1 * x2), but as the example with fit4 shows, it is not completely necessary.

Hope this is helpful!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
I am really impressed by Mike's differentiation of estimation from analysis. Here is a scenario that is really confusing to me. If I regress shape on age for a 3D object of k lanmdarks, I would obtain a vector b = (b_1x, b_1y, b_1z, b_2x, b_2y, b_2z, ..., b_kx, b_ky, b_kz). Is it appropriate to consider
(b_1x, b_1y, b_1z) as the grwoth vector for landmark 1?

Intuition tells me there is something wrong with such a claim since in this way, landmarks are interpreted one at a time. However, realizing that b is obtained through estimation rather than analysis, I cannot reject such a claim. Perhaps such a claim is appropriate?

Kieran

On Friday, January 20, 2023 at 2:00:51 AM UTC+8 mlco...@gmail.com wrote:
> From a practical perspective, Dean’s points are spot on.  It does not matter if you use Procrustes coordinates or the full set of PC scores for Procrustes ANOVA.  If performing MANOVA, then using only the PCs that have non-zero eigenvalues is essential, and a case could be made that using only a portion of the PCs that explain, e.g., 98 or 99% of the variation might be better to avoid problems with statistics that find the determinant of ill-conditioned matrices.  This is an ad hoc solution similar to what Miriam was noting, statistical limitations, not in general but with some data sets.  I’ll add two more considerations. First, if one wishes to transform a reference configuration to a target configuration based on predicted shape changes by a linear model, Procrustes coordinates are required.  This would not work with PC scores.  Second, if one has a situation where a measure of model likelihood is needed, PC scores will be in order, especially if one has many sliding landmarks (in which case some arbitrary cut-off of the number of PCs is also probably needed).  This is related to the MANOVA concern, but maybe not for statistical tests (rather for comparing models with a model selection criterion).
>
> If one is a coder, when to use coordinates or PCs might be determined by one’s need for proficiency.  For example, the default in procD.lm is turbo = TRUE.  One would choose this is they are not worried about estimating coefficients in every RRPP permutation (which requires coordinates).  In this case, PCs are used, because they are always fewer in number than the coordinates, so thousands of permutations could be performed in less time and with less burden on computer memory.  “This sounds like hair-splitting!” might say the person who has not had to worry about users hitting computational ceilings with their large, complex data sets.
>
> Cheers!
> Mike

I understand that PCA is merely a rotation of the data so it makes sense that both approaches yield identical results. As Zelditch has poited out in her Green Book, PCs should not be analyzed separately. But when all PCs are analyzed jointly, the results should be no different from directly using Procrustes shape coordinates. Hi Lucía,

I think your reasoning is good.  The combining of parts from different ANOVA tables was something I did as an example but yes, it only worked with type I SS and only if the model terms were entered in the same order.  This assures consistency with the null models for effects between the different ANOVAs.  With type II or type III SS this becomes more challenging, and since the sum of SS for effects does not equal to the total SS, it would be dangerous to combine effects from different ANOVa tables.  If you are happy with the fit4 approach — if this fulfills your desire to have combined factors for your error term and you prefer to use type III SS — then you should trust those results without worrying about combining results from different ANOVA tables.  In fact, that the SS and MS for Pop in ANOVA of fit4 is the same as in fit1 or fit2 is reassuring that the model does what it should with respect to estimating coefficients.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi, everyone,

When performing PCA on Procrustes aligned data, gm.prcomp by default does not scale columns of data. However, adding scale=T will initially scale the columns. User manual of geomorph did not mention the scale argument for gm.prcomp. None of the examples for gm.prcomp added scale=T as an argument. I am not sure if this is because it is not recommended to scale Procrustes aligned data during PCA. Any ideas?

Thank you!

Best regards
Lv

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I wish to simulate Procrustes shape coordinates for 10 3D specimens with 18 landmarks each. I want to simulate three modules of 5, 6, and 7 landmarks, respectively.

As the first step, I reconstructed the covariance matrix S following Mike and Dean's paper introducing CR coefficients. But I am stuck with how I should go on to construct Procrustes shape coordinates from the S matrix.

Here is my code:
nlm1 <- 5 #Number of landmarks in module 1
nlm2 <- 6  # Number of landmarks in module 2
nlm3 <- 7  # Number of landmarks in module 3
sw1 <- 0.4 #Within-module covariance for module 1
sw2 <- 0.5  #Within-module covariance for module 2
sw3 <- 0.6  #Within-module covariance for module 3
sb12 <- 0.1 #Covariance between module 1 and 2
sb23 <- 0.2 #Covariance between module 2 and 3
sb13 <- 0.3  #Covariance between module 1 and 3
sddig <- 0.1 #sd along diagonal of S
sigma <- 0.03 # sd for simulated values

s1 <- matrix(rnorm((3 * nlm1)^2, sw1, sigma), (3 * nlm1))
diag(s1) <- rnorm((3 * nlm1), 0, sddig)

s2 <- matrix(rnorm((3 * nlm2)^2, sw2, sigma), (3 * nlm2))
diag(s2) <- rnorm((3 * nlm2), 0, sddig)

s3 <- matrix(rnorm((3 * nlm3)^2, sw3, sigma), (3 * nlm3))
diag(s3) <- rnorm((3 * nlm3), 0, sddig)

s12 <- matrix(rnorm((3 * nlm1) * (3 * nlm2), sb12, sigma), (3 * nlm1))
s13 <- matrix(rnorm((3 * nlm1) * (3 * nlm3), sb13, sigma), (3 * nlm1))
s23 <- matrix(rnorm((3 * nlm2) * (3 * nlm3), sb23, sigma), (3 * nlm2))

S <- rbind(cbind(s1,        s12,     s13),
                  cbind(t(s12),  s2,       s23),
                  cbind(t(s13),  t(s23), s3)
                  )

Here are my questions:
1. The CR coef paper mentioned "The elements were then adjusted as needed so that the resulting matrix conformed to the properties of a valid covariance matrix (i.e. symmetric, positive definite)." While S is symmetric as above, I wonder how to code so that S is guaranteened to be positive definite?

2. If it is possible to reconstruct Procrustes shape coordinates using S matrix or some additional data? Could you please provide a simple illustrative R code?

Thank you very much for help!

Best regards,
Kieran

messages.body_plain:
Kieran,

Simulating shapes is typically accomplished with what is called the perturbation model (see Goodall 1991; Dryden and Mardia 1996, etc.). What one does is to simulate random noise at all pk landmark-coordinates, which is then added to a mean shape. Doing this repeatedly results in a sample of random shapes around the mean.  So yes, one requires the mean shape.

However, it is important to recognize that this process draws samples of random variables from a multivariate normal distribution all at once, not one variable at a time. That requires both the mean, and a covariance matrix from which the MVN distribution is defined.  The mean is easy: that is the mean shape. Generating a valid covariance matrix is rather more involved (and this is where the quote from my paper comes back in).

Procedurally, one may want a certain level of covariance within modules and a different level among modules. That is easy to represent as a square, symmetric matrix. But it may not be a valid covariance matrix (i.e., it may not be positive definite). If not, then the matrix is singular, cannot be inverted, and thus, cannot be used to define the MVN distribution from which random shapes are obtained. So in practice, one generates the desired matrix, and if it is not a valid covariance matrix, one then finds the closest valid covariance matrix to it. There are many ways of doing this, but a useful one is the ‘nearPD’ function in the Matrix library (this uses the classic algorithm of Higham 2002).

Here is a simple example of generating iid isotropic data for triangles. In practice, one would change S.in to whatever input covariance is desired.

Best,

Dean

##

library(geomorph)

library(MASS)

n = 500

p=3

k=2

var.in <http://var.in> = .005

S.in <- diag(var.in <http://var.in>,p*k)

### NOTE: one should check ‘S.in’ to ensure it is a valid covariance matrix, and if not find the nearest one

mn <- geomorph:::center.scale(matrix(c(-2,0,2,0, 0,sqrt(12)), byrow = T, ncol=2))$coords

tri <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n,mu=as.vector(t(mn)),Sigma= S.in),p = p, k = k)

Y.gpa <- gpagen(tri)

plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpa$coords)

Thank you so much Prof. Dean for your quite helpful code and explanations. They do help a lot!

The aim of my simulation is trying to have an idea of what cluster one would get if one constructs a p*p covariance of landmarks by calculating CR coef for each pair of landmarks and then do clustering on the p*p matrix. I know this approach is WRONG! Treating a single landmark as a single module essentiall removes within-module covariance. modularity.test does not fail just because of the non-zero covariance beween landmark coordinates (e.g., 1x and 1y). I would like to ask for the above simulation purpose, if it is necessary to assign different covariance values for entries describing covariance of landmark coordinates of the same landmark (e.g., 1x and 1y) and within-module between-landmark covariance ( e.g., 1x and 2y when lm 1 and 2 are in the same module)?

Additionally, just to confirm that the following code is the correct way to test modularity based on simulated dataset:

library(geomorph)
library(MASS)

n = 500

p=5

k=2

var.in <http://var.in> = .005
S.in <- diag(var.in <http://var.in>,p*k)

### NOTE: one should check ‘S.in’ to ensure it is a valid covariance matrix, and if not find the nearest one

mn <- geomorph:::center.scale(matrix(c(0, -2, -1, 1, 2, 1, 0, -1, -1, 0), byrow = F, ncol=2))$coords
pent <- arrayspecs(mvrnorm(n, mu = as.vector(t(mn)), Sigma = S.in), p = p, k = k)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(pent)
plotAllSpecimens(Y.gpa$coords)

land.gps<-rep('a',5); land.gps[3:5]<-'b'
MT <- modularity.test(Y.gpa$coords, land.gps, CI=FALSE, iter=999, opt.rot = T,
print.progress = T)

Thank you again for your clear explanations.

Best,
Kieran

Kieran,

As I stated clearly in the paper, it is nonsensical to have a single landmark as a partition. There is no covariation between landmarks in that case (only among its coordinates).

In modularity.test, we check for the number of variables per partition to ensure that a single variable is not a partition. However, because the function is for both landmark data and other data, the check is a bit further down in the routine, so it missed a single landmark situation you are trying. That is why your example ‘worked’, and slipped past us! (side-note, as programmers it is very hard to devise checks for all possible input errors that users can envision. We do our best, but some do get past us!).

I will fix this missed data check immediately and push the correction to Github.

To summarize, the question of modularity with 1 landmark per partition does not make any logical sense to investigate. I stated so clearly in the paper summarizing the method; but somehow that particular data check slipped past us.

It will be fixed within the hour.

Dean

Dear Prof. Dean,

I fully agree and understand that it is nonsensical to have a single landmark as a module.

I do such "wrong" simulation since I noted some papers in the most prestigious scientific journals are still using RV coefficient to calculate pairwise similarity between landmarks. From an empirical perspective, I am curious to learn how clustering based on such a "nonsensical" pairwise similarity matrix, as performed in the paper, would lead to clusters that are incompatible with the simulated true modules.

Perhaps clustering performed on the matrix of pairwise landmark similarity obtained from RV coefficient would result in clusters of points that are nothing but spatially more uniformly ditributed. But this could be tested through simulation IMHO.

Given that the aim of the simulation is to evaluate whether and how clustering the aforementioned matrix of RV coefs would lead to clusters incompatible with the simulated pre-specified true modules, if it is necessary to assign different covariance values for entries describing covariance of coordinates of the same landmark (e.g., 1x and 1y) and different landmarks within the same module ( e.g., 1x and 2y when lm 1 and 2 are in the same module)? Both conditions are considered "within-module" in the formula of both CR and RV coefs, but I am not sure for simulation purpose, if it is necessary to differentiate the two conditions.

I hope this explains I the background of my simulation and question. Thank you!

Best regards,
Kieran

Kieran,

I am not quite sure what answer you are expecting, as I have tried to be clear. It is nonsensical to perform a modularity analysis with a single landmark as a partition. This makes no biological, conceptual, or mathematical sense to do this. Even if one forces some computer code to do this, it is impossible to use such simulations to determine the ‘behavior’ of the method relative to expectation, as there is no expectation to be had here.

I am also unaware of any paper that used the RV coefficient with single landmarks as partitions. There are papers that attempt to evaluate variation landmark by landmark, but that is not the same thing as using the RV coefficient with a single landmark defined as a partition. Variation at a landmark is precisely that.  The RV coefficient is a ratio of relative covariation between vs within partitions. It uses the full trait covariance matrix to arrive at a single summary measure. There is not a one-to-one mapping between the two quantities.

Dean

Dear Prof. Dean,

I fully agree and understand that it is nonsensical to have a single landmark as a module.

I do such "wrong" simulation since I noted some papers in the most prestigious scientific journals are still using RV coefficient to calculate pairwise similarity between landmarks. From an empirical perspective, I am curious to learn how clustering based on such a "nonsensical" pairwise similarity matrix, as performed in the paper, would lead to clusters that are incompatible with the simulated true modules.

Perhaps clustering performed on the matrix of pairwise landmark similarity obtained from RV coefficient would result in clusters of points that are nothing but spatially more uniformly ditributed. But this could be tested through simulation IMHO.

Given that the aim of the simulation is to evaluate whether and how clustering the aforementioned matrix of RV coefs would lead to clusters incompatible with the simulated pre-specified true modules, if it is necessary to assign different covariance values for entries describing covariance of coordinates of the same landmark (e.g., 1x and 1y) and different landmarks within the same module ( e.g., 1x and 2y when lm 1 and 2 are in the same module)? Both conditions are considered "within-module" in the formula of both CR and RV coefs, but I am not sure for simulation purpose, if it is necessary to differentiate the two conditions.

I hope this explains I the background of my simulation and question. Thank you!

Best regards,

Kieran

I think there might be some conflating of the RV coefficient as a descriptive statistic and as a test statistic in a test of modularity.  It *is* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from a landmark configuration comprising two modules, one of which contains only one landmark.  The one-landmark covariance matrix would be a 2 x 2 matrix for 2d landmarks or a 3 x 3 matrix for 3d landmarks, so covariances do exist in these matrices.  But even this is a distraction.  The RV coefficient was introduced by Escoufier in 1973, not with landmarks in mind.  It *is also* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from two variables, each with covariances matrices that are single values: variances.  The RV coefficient should be the square of the correlation coefficient between the variables in such cases, which is why the RV coefficient has intuitive appeal as a multivariate generalization of correlation.

However, a test of modularity using the RV coefficient as a test statistic randomizes combinations of landmarks within modules, which is the same as randomizing the locations of variances and covariances within a covariance matrix, without changing the covariances.  But the randomization is constrained such that x, y, and possibly z covariances within landmarks  cannot be changed (the coordinates are not randomized between landmarks).  Although one *could* calculate an RV coefficient in every random permutation that assigns a landmark randomly to be a one-landmark module, the distribution of RV coefficients from this process would be meaningless for evaluating any null hypothesis about modularity.  If the point is to illustrate the meaninglessness from a simulation, I would argue that the simulation experiment is not needed, as its purpose is invalid, based on first principles.

Dean’s point was a simulation forced to find RV coefficients from random one-landmark modules will produce distributions fraught with misinterpretation.  Unless there is at least one pair of landmarks — and even then, be careful of spurious results! — a test of modularity just should not be considered.  The RV coefficient might still be a descriptive statistic, but it cannot be considered an appropriate test statistic in tests involving one-landmark modules.

Mike

Kieran et al.,

The problem with the simulation-based application being discussed is the expectation that simulating data of some known form will return a particular RV value out the back end of the analysis. There is simply no way to know what RV value is ‘expected’, regardless of how one simulates the input data.  In my 2016 paper (also Smilde et al. 2009) I showed that for random data, the expected value of RV changes with both sample size (N) and the number of variables (p). Thus, even under the simplest of conditions it cannot be known what RV value is ‘expected’. So how can anyone a priori claim to know what the RV should be for some set of simulated data? They cannot.

Now add the mathematical reality that the RV coefficient is a measure that summarize variation and covariation from a partitioned covariance matrix, and does so in a particular manner. Specifically, the RV is a measure of the RELATIVE covariation between partitions versus within them  (in text ~ Sb / Sw). That is not the same as describing variation at a single landmark, and it does NOT equate perfectly to the variation at a single landmark. This is the case even if a single landmark is used as a partition, because the RV in this case is 1 landmark vs. all others. In other words, RV is not isolating the variation at that landmark: again a flaw of the logic being applied.

Since there is no one-to-one mapping of variation at a single landmark and the RV coefficient for that landmark vs. the rest, the simulation has no expected outcome that can be stated beforehand. Any outcome obtained cannot be judged reliably versus what might be expected, because the latter does not exist.

I don’t know how to make this any more clear. The logic that underlies the simulation does not make any sense.

Dean

I have two comments to make as a follow-up.  Thanks to Kieran for a detailed private message that clears up what the purpose of the methods used in the papers he provided.  I feel I can comment more specifically on what was intended and whether it was correct.  I have two comments to make.

First, the purpose of the analysis is not a test but rather a descriptive procedure.  For a configuration of p points in k dimensions, find the RV coefficient between all pairs of p_i, p_j landmarks and record this value in a matrix.  All values would be positive and presumably measure the strength of association between landmarks.  One could image the matrix like a heat map and find the areas in the configuration where there are clusters of highly associated points.  On the surface this seems like a good tool, and because it uses portions of a covariance matrix that have been established after GPA, it is not a one-at-a-time kind of landmark analysis.

However this approach is fundamentally flawed (even if it was published).  The RV coefficient standardizes covariances by joint variances and because those variances will vary among landmark pairs, the method of standardization is incommensurate across landmarks.  It is possible to find landmarks with higher covariation but lower correlation because the pairs have different landmark variances, which should be taken also with a grain of salt since they are portions of configurations from a procedure that intended to minimize variance globally, not locally.

The numerator of each RV coefficient is the sum of squared singular values in the between-landmark covariances.  The denominators are the products of the sums of eigenvalues within landmark covariance matrices.  I might buy that this procedure is a valid thing to do if only the numerator squared singular values were used for comparative purposes, or they were standardized by a common value, like the sum of eigenvalues for the entire matrix.  But with RV coefficients estimated without regard to other landmarks, spurious results should be typical.

Second comment, speaking of spurious results, I would really like to start a campaign that GPA does not induce spurious results.  I know some of our colleagues have published papers about the peril of GM data and test of modularity/integration but I feel there has been a tendency to blame the messenger for providing data that already had true spatial covariances that were not independent before GPA.  Having many anatomical points in close proximity, perhaps for the same structure, means having strong spatial covariances among those points.  GPA does not create those covariances.  If anything, GPA might buffer their true strength by finding means of those points after rotation, thus making the landmarks less spatially related for the mean than for any single configuration.

We need to let go of thinking that data subjected to GPA come out with induced modularity or integration.  It will be possible, however, to misinterpret modularity and integration by performing analyses on parts of configurations rather than the entire configurations.  Finding the RV coefficient by landmark pairs is one way to do this.  I have no qualms with finding the eigenvalues of cross-products by pair, however, as long as they come from data from the same GPA.  This does not change the global solution.  The p * (p - 1) / 2 separate standardization methods in the RV coefficients does.

Cheers!
Mike

> On Feb 22, 2023, at 9:30 AM, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I think there might be some conflating of the RV coefficient as a descriptive statistic and as a test statistic in a test of modularity.  It *is* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from a landmark configuration comprising two modules, one of which contains only one landmark.  The one-landmark covariance matrix would be a 2 x 2 matrix for 2d landmarks or a 3 x 3 matrix for 3d landmarks, so covariances do exist in these matrices.  But even this is a distraction.  The RV coefficient was introduced by Escoufier in 1973, not with landmarks in mind.  It *is also* possible to estimate an RV coefficient from two variables, each with covariances matrices that are single values: variances.  The RV coefficient should be the square of the correlation coefficient between the variables in such cases, which is why the RV coefficient has intuitive appeal as a multivariate generalization of correlation.
>
> However, a test of modularity using the RV coefficient as a test statistic randomizes combinations of landmarks within modules, which is the same as randomizing the locations of variances and covariances within a covariance matrix, without changing the covariances.  But the randomization is constrained such that x, y, and possibly z covariances within landmarks  cannot be changed (the coordinates are not randomized between landmarks).  Although one *could* calculate an RV coefficient in every random permutation that assigns a landmark randomly to be a one-landmark module, the distribution of RV coefficients from this process would be meaningless for evaluating any null hypothesis about modularity.  If the point is to illustrate the meaninglessness from a simulation, I would argue that the simulation experiment is not needed, as its purpose is invalid, based on first principles.
>
> Dean’s point was a simulation forced to find RV coefficients from random one-landmark modules will produce distributions fraught with misinterpretation.  Unless there is at least one pair of landmarks — and even then, be careful of spurious results! — a test of modularity just should not be considered.  The RV coefficient might still be a descriptive statistic, but it cannot be considered an appropriate test statistic in tests involving one-landmark modules.

> > > > > However, it is important to recognize that this process draws samples of random variables from a multivariate normal distribution all at once, not one variable at a time. That requires both the mean, and a covariance matrix from which the MVN distribution is defined.  The mean is easy: that is the mean shape. Generating a valid covariance matrix is rather more involved (and this is where the quote from my paper comes back in).
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Procedurally, one may want a certain level of covariance within modules and a different level among modules. That is easy to represent as a square, symmetric matrix. So in practice, one generates the desired matrix, and if it is not a valid covariance matrix, one then finds the closest valid covariance matrix to it.
